title: What agentic workflows require of people and organisations · hancrafted
description: A working definition of agentic workflows; how people choose oversight task by task and can review outcomes; useful capabilities for planning, handoffs and checks; and organisational conditions that can support goal-led workflows. The examples are illustrative, not universal rules, and handoff gaps are not automatically individual failures.

What an agentic workflow is (2/2) Page 2 of 2 What an agentic workflow is Working definition for this Episode: agents take some decisions and actions inside a path people set. This combines vendor descriptions; it is not universal. You design the path; the agent steers inside its task. You design this the stages, their order, what each hands over, where you sign off Use case : Plan a summer party Stages Jobs Practice it for Plan Plan → four work areas; Venue and date first Get interviewed, then a short plan of epics Practice it for Requirements Requirements → signed-off needs, checks and research questions Grill one epic, then sign off its tickets checked You sign off Practice it for Research Research → sourced findings; gaps stay open Research 1 Research 2 One fresh chat per ticket Practice it for Page Page → one page: the party plan Gather it, then one page to sign off You sign off Explore it → → four work areas; Venue and date first → signed-off needs, checks and research questions → sourced findings; gaps stay open → one page: the party plan The agent steers this Agent You set its task: research each ticket in its own fresh chat, with web search and a source for every number. How it gets there is its own call. Search the web → Compare 3 venues → Note a source per number until it thinks it is done “Minimal human intervention” Here you sign off twice. How minimal, and for which task? The next Section answers it.
How far you step out How much of a person stays in is a choice you make per task. in on out Food & drinks Venue kitchen a person on the loop checks the menu

How far you step out (1/2) Page 1 of 2 In, on or out of the loop Three levels of human oversight, set per task: the same workflow keeps a person in for one task, on for another and out for a third. Chosen per task In the loop Human in the loop · HITL The agent acts only after a person approves. The gatekeeper approves each step On the loop Human on the loop · HOTL It acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. The pilot watches, steps in on exceptions Out of the loop Human out of the loop · HOOTL No one intervenes during the task; a person may still review its result afterwards. The auditor may review the result or logs afterwards One task, three ways Venue · Book a venue for 200 on 20 June Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely Agent In the loop Proposes a venue Nothing is booked until you say yes. Agent On the loop Books the venue and reports You read the reports and step in if something looks wrong. Agent Out of the loop Books the venue You get the confirmation. Risk of a wrong result: depends on the task and its context Speed highest where nobody waits Borrowed terms The words: military policy on weapon autonomy, 2012 The concept: supervisory control in aircraft

How far you step out (2/2) Page 2 of 2 Reviewability sets the distance For each task, consider both the impact of a wrong result and how well it can be checked. This is a useful synthesis, not a universal formula. Summer party · illustrative choices, not defaults; risk and checkability are two considerations Agent Guest list 200 names, 5 offices If wrong: a name missing, fixed with one email Checked by: count against each office's staff list, no person needed Out of the loop 200 guests Agent Venue A venue for 200 on 20 June If wrong: 200 people at a place that doesn't fit Checked by: capacity, date, access, read in the reports On the loop venue, date Agent Activity One activity for 200 Was: Paintball × 200, only your yes or no If wrong: colleagues left out of the day In On the loop Its check, built in Everyone can join Wheelchair access No fitness needed programme Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely My hypothesis: weighing risk and checkability together is a synthesis, not one source's rule ( ) , and the evidence for checkability comes mostly from software ( ) .

What it requires of each person Four failures, three missing skills, and each skill has a name. Food & drinks Venue kitchen Receives 200 guests, 31 vegetarian Delivers dinner for 200, 19:00 Checked by menu vs definition = no meat, fish or eggs

What it requires of each person (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Plan back from the goal Backward reasoning starts from the goal and breaks it into what must be true before it, until it reaches where you stand today. Must be true before that Must be true just before Start here Venue Alpine hut, 1,800 m External The hut’s kitchen Not yours to change Subgoal Everyone celebrates together New Shuttle back after the open bar The drivers can drink New in guest info Bring warm clothes, 6 °C at night Nobody arrives cold Subgoal Everyone gets home safely Goal, as an outcome 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely State the goal as an outcome. It tells you when you are done. Mark what is outside your control. Plan around it. Look for tasks the draft left unowned. In this example, they appear under a subgoal. Well known Project management: the backward pass of the Critical Path Method schedules back from a fixed completion date ( ) Agents: they do better with a clearly defined goal and outcome ( ) ; left unstated, it costs accuracy ( )

What it requires of each person (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Reviewing the result Verification checks a result against its contract; validation checks it against the goal. This example uses a person for the goal check; appropriate checks can also be automated. What it requires of the organisation (1/4) Page 1 of 4 The org chart trap Conway’s law is a useful hypothesis: designs often reflect who talks to whom. A workflow people draw for themselves is also a design. Party committee · org chart Committee lead Venue scouts 10 people Caterer 1 person Travel planner 1 person copies Their draft AI workflow Venue scouting · 14 steps 1 Brief the scouts 2 List regions 3 Long-list venues 4 Call 40 venues 5 Check dates 6 Visit north 7 Visit south 8 Score venues 9 Compare prices 10 Second visits 11 Shortlist 3 12 Present 13 Vote 14 Book venue Catering · 1 step Order 200 meals Travel · 1 step Book trains Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely No step plans back from here. “Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization’s communication structure.” Melvin Conway, 1968 ( ) A tendency, not a rule: strong in 70% of firm studies ( ) Applying it to workflows is my inference, not a measured result. The first design may not be best: test it against the goal ( )

What it requires of the organisation (2/4) Page 2 of 4 Designed AI first One possible redesign starts from the goal, makes handoffs checkable and removes steps that add no reviewable value. Illustrative before · committee-shaped draft, 16 steps Venue scouting · 14 Catering · 1 Travel · 1 shaped by the org chart One possible redraw from the goal: 5 notes, a contract on every arrow agent Travel + guest info, merged 3 Delivers route, times, accessible bus, warm clothes for 6 °C Checked: info against the venue agent Venue: alpine hut, step-free Delivers address, step-free entry Checked: a person, at a checkpoint ( ) agent Food & drinks for 200 Receives 31 vegetarian: no meat, fish or eggs Delivers dinner for 200 at 19:00 Checked: the menu against the definition How: the kitchen’s choice 2 person Activities everyone can join Delivers a programme for all 200, step-free Checked: against the goal agent Shuttle back after the open bar Delivers everyone home, nobody drives Checked: shuttle list against guests Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely 1 Outcome: 200 guests from 5 offices, all home safe 1 Start at the outcome. Roles say who is free; the outcome says what is needed. 2 Make handoffs checkable , while leaving the inside of a task open ( ) . 3 Simplify unhelpful handoffs. Merge steps that add no reviewable value ( ) . In this example, better handoffs—not more meetings—close the gaps.

What it requires of the organisation (3/4) Page 3 of 4 What did you need to do? Three useful capabilities to develop, synthesized from this party example, alongside an organisation designed around the goal. Useful capabilities Break the work down from the goal Carpools + open bar a shuttle back, nobody drives 1,800 m in summer clothes guest info: warm clothes, 6 °C at night Write the contract at the seam “31 vegetarian” got egg dishes defined: no meat, fish or eggs Review against contract and goal ( ) Paintball × 200 an activity the ten wheelchair users join From the organisation Clear goals An outcome you can measure, like “everyone home safe”. Contracts between teams Receives, delivers, checked by, at every seam. An oversight policy per task In the loop On the loop Out of the loop Workflows around the goal Not around the org chart. This three-skill set is a synthesis from the example, not a tested universal checklist ( ) . Junior colleagues may have fewer chances to practise narrow tasks when agents take them over ( ) .

What it requires of the organisation (4/4) Page 4 of 4 One whole workflow Follow the summer-party workflow from goal to plan. These are illustrative oversight choices, not defaults; use the level that fits each task. 3 Goal: bring 200 people from five offices together next summer, within €60,000 Use case : Plan a summer party Stages Jobs Demo mode Practice it for Plan Plan Get interviewed, then a short plan of epics On the loop 1 Plan → Requirements Receives the party goal and constraints Delivers four work areas, Venue and date first Checked by: the priority fits the goal 2 Practice it for Requirements Requirements Grill one epic, then sign off its tickets checked Gate 1 In the loop Requirements → Research Receives the chosen Venue and date work area Delivers needs, checks and research questions Checked by: the organiser signs off this set Practice it for Research Research On the loop Research 1 Research 2 One fresh chat per ticket Research → Page Receives signed-off checks and research questions Delivers sourced venue, travel and date findings Checked by: sources support claims; gaps stay open Practice it for Page Page Gather it, then one page to sign off Gate 2 In the loop 4 Explore it → You design the stages; the agent steers inside each task 1 Pick one recurring process. Mark each step: agent or person, in, on or out of the loop. “Out” means no intervention during that task. 2 Write the handoff clearly. What the task receives and delivers, and how its result can be checked; checks need not all be human. 3 Use Conway’s law as a prompt. If team boundaries make handoffs work against the goal, consider another design. 4 Develop useful capabilities. Breaking work down, writing clear handoffs and checking results.

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

The thought experiment A real version of the board Anthropic's lead agent gave its subagents vague task descriptions, and they duplicated each other's searches and left gaps until each task carried an objective, an output format, tool guidance and boundaries; one team's account of its own system, not a controlled comparison 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Now with agents One model trained only on public datasets The LLaMA authors set out to show that state-of-the-art models could be trained using publicly available datasets exclusively; this describes that model's training, not every model 1 . Sources (1) Touvron et al., LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Anthropic excludes commercial data by default Anthropic says it does not use inputs or outputs from its commercial products for training by default. For those products, internal processes, decisions and naming are not automatically part of the model's training data; other providers and settings may differ 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Is my data used for model training? (commercial products) ( opens in a new tab ) privacy.claude.com Rare facts can be harder to recall In the studied factual-question benchmarks, answer accuracy tracked how many training documents mentioned a fact. That finding does not mean every rare fact is absent or every model behaves alike 1 . Sources (1) Kandpal et al., Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Context can be retrieved at request time Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a model with searchable memory that can be consulted when a request runs. Relevant organisational knowledge can therefore be supplied or retrieved at task time rather than assumed to be in training data 1 . Sources (1) Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org
What an agentic workflow is No speaker notes for this Slide.

What an agent is Anthropic's definition Agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, keeping control over how they accomplish tasks 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com A shorter form “An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal”, with a stopping condition 1 . Sources (1) Willison, I think “agent” may finally have a widely enough agreed upon definition ( opens in a new tab ) simonwillison.net

What an agentic workflow is IBM's wording “Agentic workflows are AI-driven processes where autonomous AI agents make decisions, take actions and coordinate tasks with minimal human intervention.” 1 Sources (1) Gutowska and Stryker (IBM), What are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) ibm.com Salesforce's wording “Agentic workflows are structured processes where AI agents make decisions, solve problems, and perform tasks with minimal human input.” The word “structured” is Salesforce's; “coordinate tasks” is IBM's. The Slide's sentence merges the two and belongs to neither vendor 1 . Sources (1) Salesforce, What Are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) salesforce.com Why the vendors stress autonomy Both sell agent platforms and praise reduced oversight; that this explains their wording is an inference, the pages give no reason 1 . Sources (1) Gutowska and Stryker (IBM), What are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) ibm.com Two levels of control Anthropic draws the line at who controls the steps: workflows are orchestrated through predefined code paths, agents direct their own process. Applying “you design the path, the agent steers inside its task” to a team's process is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Autonomy as a degree Ng prefers to call systems agent-like to different degrees, with a gray zone, over a binary 1 . Sources (1) Andrew Ng, The Batch issue 253 (letter on agentic workflows) ( opens in a new tab ) deeplearning.ai
How far you step out No speaker notes for this Slide.

In, on or out of the loop Origin of the three terms the triad comes from a 2012 report on weapon autonomy: in the loop means force only with a human command, on the loop means under a human operator who can override, out of the loop means without any human input 1 . Sources (1) Human Rights Watch and Harvard IHRC, Losing Humanity (19 Nov 2012) ( opens in a new tab ) hrw.org Two senses of "on" the EU 2019 ethics guidelines define on the loop as intervening during design and monitoring operation, which differs from the military override sense used here; the guidelines have no out-of-the-loop term 1 . Sources (1) EU High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (8 Apr 2019) ( opens in a new tab ) ec.europa.eu Approving to monitoring experienced users shift from approving individual actions to monitoring the agent and intervening when needed 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Out is a per-step property no source claims a person is out of the loop for a whole lifecycle; the humans move to specs and outcome checks 1 . Sources (1) Willison, How StrongDM's AI team build serious software without even looking at the code ( opens in a new tab ) simonwillison.net Regulation limits out for high-risk uses, EU AI Act Article 14 requires that a person can override and stop the system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Aviation supplied the concept, not the words Sheridan traces supervisory control to computers replacing direct manual control in aircraft, which left the person "in a new role of monitor and goal-constraint setter"; no source traces the words "in, on, out of the loop" to aviation, they come from the military policy above 1 . Sources (1) Sheridan, Human Supervisory Control (Handbook of Systems Engineering and Management, Wiley, 1999, ch. 16) ( opens in a new tab ) hlaszny.com Levels are not a strict ladder the FAA warns that describing automation as a linear hierarchy of levels is difficult to apply operationally, and that responsibility for flightpath management stays with the pilots at all times; it concerns airline pilots, so carrying it to agents is an analogy 1 . Sources (1) FAA, Advisory Circular 120-123, Flightpath Management (21 Nov 2022) ( opens in a new tab ) faa.gov

Reviewability sets the distance Software is easy to check "Software is unusually amenable to supervisory oversight because the outputs can be tested"; where checking needs the expertise that producing took, trust may build more slowly 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Vigilance is no check complacency and automation bias occur in naive and expert people and are not removed by training or instructions, so the check must be built into the result 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman and Manzey, Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration (Human Factors 52(3), 2010) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Level is a design choice the level of automation is set per function, judged by human performance consequences and the cost of errors, which is why a task may stay in for reasons other than checkability 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Oversight follows risk in the rules the EU AI Act requires oversight measures "commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use" of a high-risk system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Risk as a tool rating OpenAI tells builders to rate each tool low, medium or high by factors such as read-only versus write access, reversibility and financial impact, and to trigger human oversight for sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes actions until confidence in the agent grows 1 . Sources (1) OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents ( opens in a new tab ) cdn.openai.com Risk is one input, not the rule no source says risk alone decides the level; the aviation-derived model ranks the effect on human performance first and the cost of errors second, so combining risk and checkability into one per-task choice is a synthesis 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org
What it requires of each person No speaker notes for this Slide.

Plan back from the goal Pappus and Pólya analysis starts from what is required, takes it for granted, and asks from what antecedent it could be derived, until it reaches something already known; Pólya’s entry calls it “working backwards” 1 . Sources (1) Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards ( opens in a new tab ) hlevkin.com Regression in planning in AI planning, each backward step adds the action’s preconditions to the goal, and each precondition is a dependency the plan needs 1 . Sources (1) Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning ( opens in a new tab ) aima.cs.berkeley.edu Fewer actions to consider backward search considers only relevant actions; in the textbook air cargo problem about 1000 actions lead forward and 20 work backward, for that one problem only 1 . Sources (1) Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning ( opens in a new tab ) aima.cs.berkeley.edu It feels wrong Pólya notes a psychological difficulty in turning around and not following the direct path to the end 1 . Sources (1) Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards ( opens in a new tab ) hlevkin.com Project management does it too in the Critical Path Method, Kelley and Walker compute the latest time each event may occur “relative to a fixed project completion time”; neither this paper nor the NASA handbook uses the phrase “backward pass”, which is later textbook vocabulary 1 . Sources (1) Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959) ( opens in a new tab ) mosaicprojects.com.au What the backward run gives a job whose maximum available time equals its duration is critical, because a delay in it delays the project; the method takes the jobs and dependencies as given and is not shown to find missing tasks, so that use here is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959) ( opens in a new tab ) mosaicprojects.com.au Scope starts at the end product the NASA handbook says a work breakdown structure begins with the end item and successively subdivides it, and calls it “a product-oriented structure, not an organizational structure” 1 . Sources (1) Sadler, NASA Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Handbook (NASA/SP-20250006071) ( opens in a new tab ) nasa.gov Vendors say: clear goals Anthropic names the best-fit tasks for agents as those with clear success criteria and feedback loops, such as code that automated tests can verify; this is guidance, not a measurement 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Missing detail costs accuracy models infer unstated requirements 41.1% of the time, prompts that omit requirements are twice as likely to regress when the model or prompt changes, and accuracy sometimes drops by more than 20% 1 . Sources (1) Yang et al., What Prompts Don’t Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Asking recovers it, and the limit on an underspecified coding benchmark, interacting to ask questions gained up to 74% over not asking, a ceiling and not an average; no source isolates a clear goal as a single variable, so the claim is that missing detail hurts and recovering it helps 1 . Sources (1) Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Contracts at the seams A contract has two sides Meyer’s model is the business contract: each party expects benefits and accepts obligations to obtain them, documented in a contract document 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu Pre- and postcondition the precondition states what any call must satisfy, the postcondition what the call ensures in return; each condition belongs to exactly one party 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu No defensive duplication either the condition is guaranteed by the client or handled by the supplier; checking everything on both sides adds complexity 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu Same split in Eiffel Eiffel Software defines a precondition as what must be true before a component is used and a postcondition as what it guarantees after execution 1 . Sources (1) Eiffel Software, Design by Contract ( opens in a new tab ) eiffel.com

Reviewing the result Two definitions Boehm defines verification as establishing the correspondence between a software product and its specification, and validation as establishing its fitness or worth for its operational mission 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com His two questions “Am I building the product right?” for verification and “Am I building the right product?” for validation 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com Where the fix lands a failed verification changes the product; a failed validation can change the requirements themselves 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com Software practice, not agents NASA words the same pair as “Are we building the product right?”; applying it to work handed to an agent is an inference 1 . Sources (1) NASA, IV&V Overview ( opens in a new tab ) nasa.gov
What it requires of the organisation No speaker notes for this Slide.

The org chart trap The law as Conway states it "Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure" 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, Conway's Law (author's page) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com Why it happens organising the team already makes design decisions, and two parts of a design can depend on each other only where their designers talked 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, How Do Committees Invent? (Datamation, April 1968) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com A tendency, not a rule a review of 142 empirical studies found mirroring a prevalent pattern but not universal: strong in 70% of industry and firm studies, absent in 56% of open collaborative projects 1 . Sources (1) Colfer and Baldwin, The mirroring hypothesis: theory, evidence, and exceptions (Industrial and Corporate Change, 2016) ( opens in a new tab ) dash.harvard.edu Components include tasks the same review defines the components of a technical system as all the tasks and decisions required to design, operate and maintain it 1 . Sources (1) Colfer and Baldwin, The mirroring hypothesis: theory, evidence, and exceptions (Industrial and Corporate Change, 2016) ( opens in a new tab ) dash.harvard.edu The first design is not the best Conway himself says the first design is almost never the best possible, so the organisation must stay flexible 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, How Do Committees Invent? (Datamation, April 1968) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com

Designed AI first Checkpoints in the path Anthropic's agent guidance has agents pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Contract-first decomposition a delegation framework makes delegation contingent on the outcome having precise verification, and splits a subtask further when its output is too costly or subjective to verify 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Vague handoffs duplicate work Anthropic's research system produced duplicated work and gaps until each subagent had an objective, an output format, tool guidance and clear task boundaries 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

What to look for in your team Management 101 skills "If you can explain what you need, give effective feedback, and design ways of evaluating work, you are going to be able to work with agents" 1 . Sources (1) Mollick, Management as AI Superpower (One Useful Thing, 27 January 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) oneusefulthing.org Effort moves to steering and checking in a survey of 319 knowledge workers, critical thinking moved toward information verification, response integration and task stewardship 1 . Sources (1) Lee et al. (Carnegie Mellon, Microsoft Research), The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) microsoft.com Evidence is indirect no source tests breaking work down, writing handoffs and reviewing results as a set, and none measures how many people can do them; that these are the skills to build is a synthesis 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Juniors may not build them the narrow tasks through which juniors build judgement are those most likely to be offloaded to agents 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

One whole workflow Workflow and agent, two levels Anthropic separates workflows, orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents that direct their own process; reading the quiz example as a path you design with steps the agent steers is an application of that split, not a claim the source makes 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

script.text: This panel shows the speaker notes and voice script for the Slide you are reading, and follows you as you scroll. Press Alt+N to open or close it.

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:24 Imagine the board Imagine you are the manager of a summer party for 200 colleagues from five offices, and you have hired four excellent freelancers to plan it, one each for Activities, Travel, Venue and Food and drinks. They never meet and they never call each other, because the only thing they share is a board where everyone leaves notes.

The thought experiment 0:00 – 0:21 Everyone delivered Now the day arrives, and every one of the four has done exactly what was asked. Activities booked a team-building event, Travel arranged how everyone gets there, Venue found a place, and Food and drinks ordered dinner. Each card is ticked, and each freelancer met their own goal perfectly. 0:21 – 1:15 None of it adds up And still the party fails, because the gaps sit between the cards—not because anyone failed at their own task. Activities booked paintball, while Travel had arranged an accessible bus for ten wheelchair users, who now cannot join. Travel set up carpools, while Food and drinks booked an open bar until one in the morning, leaving drivers with alcohol. Venue found a scenic alpine hut, but Travel's guest information gave only route and times, so people arrive in summer clothes for six degrees at night. And the food note said “31 vegetarian” without defining whether eggs were allowed; the hut kitchen included them, leaving guests who avoid eggs without a suitable meal. Each card was completed, but the handoffs did not add up to the shared goal. 1:15 – 1:47 Your question So here is the question, and I want you to keep it in your head for the whole Episode. What do you, as the manager, need to do so the result still comes out great? One tempting answer is to get the four talking, to hold more meetings. I will leave the question open for now, and we will answer it step by step, from different angles, until we collect the answers at the end.

Now with agents 0:00 – 0:22 Speed, not context Now give the same four cards to agents. In this thought experiment, each card is ticked much faster, while the handoff gaps remain. That is an illustration, not a measured universal speedup. An agent also cannot reliably use private constraints it cannot access, and the paintball agent never saw the accessible bus. 0:22 – 0:48 Plausible guess When context is missing, an agent may fill the gap with a plausible guess instead of asking. In our food example, no one specified whether eggs were allowed, so the kitchen's interpretation did not fit those guests. The example reaches the same four handoff failures in two minutes instead of two weeks; those timings illustrate the scenario, not a general benchmark.
What an agentic workflow is 0:00 – 0:12 Name the thing Before we fix the board, we need two terms to stand on. What is an agent, and what makes a workflow agentic? Term first, then the board.

What an agent is 0:00 – 0:23 Model, tools, loop An agent is a language model that uses tools in a loop and decides for itself how to reach a goal. It is not a single chat answer you read and move on from, it is a loop of acting, looking at the result and acting again until it believes it is done. 0:23 – 0:51 Steers its own steps If you have only used a chat tool so far, here is the shift. In a chat you steer every step yourself, because you read each answer and decide what to ask next. An agent steers its own steps, so you cannot assume it takes the steps you would have taken. The rest of this Episode asks what people and organisations can design around that difference.

What an agentic workflow is 0:00 – 0:18 The definition For this Episode, an agentic workflow is a process where agents take some decisions and actions inside a path people set. That is a working definition informed by vendor descriptions, not a universal standard. The exact sources are in the Speaker notes. 0:18 – 0:36 Two levels Read it as two levels. You design the path: the tasks and what each hands over to the next. The agent steers inside its own task. How much oversight each task gets is a separate choice, not something the definition settles. 0:36 – 0:53 Minimal, how minimal Notice the phrase minimal human intervention: it carries a lot of weight but does not say how much or for which task. Here, people sign off twice. The next Section looks at how oversight can be chosen task by task.

How far you step out 0:00 – 0:18 Open question The definition left one thing open, which is how much of a person stays in the workflow. That is not one setting for the whole company, it is a choice you make for each task, and it is the next thing to learn.

In, on or out of the loop 0:00 – 0:15 In Human in the loop means the agent acts only after a person has approved. Take booking the venue for the party: the agent proposes a venue, and nothing is booked until you say yes. 0:15 – 0:31 On Human on the loop means the agent acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. Now the agent books the venue itself, you read its reports, and you step in when something looks wrong. 0:31 – 0:45 Out Out of the loop means no person intervenes while this task runs. Someone can still review the result afterwards; in this example, the agent books the venue and you receive a confirmation. 0:45 – 1:07 Borrowed terms These three terms were borrowed from automation outside AI, from fields where an automated action often cannot be undone, so what role the person plays was decided on purpose and not left to chance. The detail is in the Speaker notes. We borrow them because the question is the same for your agents. 1:07 – 1:18 Per task People choose a level for each task; it is not one setting for a whole company. Consider the task's consequences, context and any applicable rules.

Reviewability sets the distance 0:00 – 0:17 The rule As a design heuristic, ask how well a result can be checked and what a wrong result could do. Neither factor sets the level by itself: people choose the oversight that fits the task, its context and applicable rules. 0:17 – 0:35 Hypothesis, said openly The rule that you can step out only as far as you can check is my hypothesis, and I say so openly; the evidence for it comes mostly from software, so treat it as a good bet and not as a law. 0:35 – 0:45 Risk too This is a synthesis, not a rule from one source. A higher-impact mistake may call for closer oversight, but context and other constraints matter too. 0:45 – 1:01 Make it checkable One useful design move is to build a check into the task: everyone can join, wheelchair access, no fitness needed. With a check like that, people could choose to monitor this activity instead of approving every step.

What it requires of each person 0:00 – 0:18 Skills behind the failures Let's go back to the board. Each of the four failures came from a skill that was missing in a person, and there are three skills in all. Each one has a name, and we take them one at a time.

Plan back from the goal 0:00 – 0:22 Start at the goal Start with the goal and work backwards. Backward reasoning is a plain-language name for something Pólya calls working backwards and AI planning calls regression. You ask what must be true just before the goal, then what must be true before that, and you repeat until you arrive at where you stand today. 0:22 – 0:38 State the outcome Write the goal as an outcome and not as an activity. Not book a venue, but everyone celebrates together and gets home safely, because an outcome tells you when you are done and an activity does not. 0:38 – 0:57 Outside your control Next, sort what the plan depends on into what is inside your control and what is outside it. The venue's kitchen is not yours, you cannot change how it works, so you plan around it and make sure whatever you hand it is unmistakable. 0:57 – 1:27 The tasks nobody owned Now work back from gets home safely. In this example, that points to a gap in the draft: people need a ride home after an open bar, so a shuttle is added. Working back from arrival also suggests telling guests to bring warm clothes for six degrees at night. Those are useful questions to ask of this plan, not a guarantee that backward planning will uncover every missing task. 1:27 – 1:46 Well known, and agents like it Planning back from a goal is a familiar project-planning idea. Agent guidance also recommends clear goals and success criteria, though that is guidance rather than a universal measurement. When you hand an agent a task, have you given it the goal or only the activity?

Contracts at the seams 0:00 – 0:14 Design by contract Meyer's design-by-contract model describes obligations and benefits between parties. Applying that idea to a team or agent handoff is a practical lens, not a rule that every task needs the same contract. 0:14 – 0:28 Receives, delivers, checked by For a handoff that matters, try writing three lines: what the next task receives, what it delivers and how the result can be checked. Keep the contract as specific as the goal requires. 0:28 – 0:51 Leave the how open Notice what the contract leaves out, and that is how the work is done. How the menu gets cooked is the kitchen's choice. That is my reading of design by contract, Meyer does not say it in these words, but it is why a contract stays short enough to write for every handoff. 0:51 – 1:12 The egg dishes Now the egg dishes. The fact 31 vegetarian travelled from one card to the other without a single error, but the word meant something else on each side. With a definition, no meat, fish or eggs, and a check of the menu against it, the egg dishes cannot arrive quietly.

Reviewing the result 0:00 – 0:15 Two checks Borrowing two software concepts, we can ask two different questions of a result. Verification checks it against its contract; validation checks whether it serves the goal. Applying those terms to agent work is an analogy. 0:15 – 0:32 Paintball passes The paintball note passes every line of its contract: an activity for 200, within budget, on the right day. And it still fails the goal, because the contract was right about what was asked and wrong about what was needed. 0:32 – 0:49 The goal check In this example, a person checks the broader goal, not just the task note. Other checks can be automated where that fits. People choose the oversight, and can review the outcome even when they did not intervene during the task. 0:49 – 1:00 Your verdict So the next time an agent hands you a result that matches its task perfectly, ask yourself which of the two checks you have actually done.

What it requires of the organisation 0:00 – 0:12 From people to the company Skills in your people are not enough. The workflow they draw has a shape of its own, and that shape comes from the organisation they work in.

The org chart trap 0:00 – 0:14 Conway's law Conway's 1968 law describes a tendency for designs to reflect communication structures. Applying it to workflows is an inference, not a measured rule; the exact wording and evidence are in the Speaker notes. 0:14 – 0:34 A team's draft I saw this with a team I worked with. They drew their AI workflow, and one discipline ended up with fourteen discovery steps while the others got one or two. The workflow mirrored the headcount, not the goal. I will not name the company or the team. 0:34 – 0:51 Broadly defined Conway meant systems in a wide sense, but applying that to workflows is my inference; the evidence does not establish a universal pattern. Treat it as a prompt to examine whether team boundaries help or hinder the goal. 0:51 – 1:03 Your sign If a workflow mirrors your org chart, use Conway's law as a prompt: are the team boundaries helping meet the goal? Consider a redesign if they get in the way.

Designed AI first 0:00 – 0:16 Start at the outcome Here is one possible response to the party example. Start from the intended outcome, rather than copying today's roles into the workflow. The roles tell you who is available; the outcome helps show what the plan needs. 0:16 – 0:31 Contract on every milestone Then make the important handoffs checkable, without prescribing every step inside the task. Agree what needs to arrive and how the result can be checked; the person or agent doing the work can choose how. 0:31 – 0:42 Cut seams Finally, look for handoffs that add no reviewable value. In this example, combining related work is one possible redesign—not a rule that fewer steps are always better. 0:42 – 0:55 Not more meetings Remember the question from the first Slide? More meetings were one possible answer. In this example, clearer goals and handoffs address the gaps; another workflow may need something else.

What to look for in your team 0:00 – 0:11 The answer In this party example, three useful capabilities might help address the gaps. This is a synthesis, not a universal checklist for every person or team. 0:11 – 0:21 Break down First, work back from the goal. In this example, that helps assign someone to plan the ride home and tell guests what to wear. 0:21 – 0:33 Write contracts Second, clarify important handoffs: what a task receives and delivers, and how its result can be checked. Here, defining the dietary requirement would help avoid the egg-dish mismatch. 0:33 – 0:43 Review twice Third, check results against both the agreed task and the broader goal. In this example, that could flag an activity some guests cannot join. 0:43 – 0:54 The organisation The organisation also shapes the conditions: clear goals, useful handoffs, task-specific oversight choices and workflows designed around the goal rather than the org chart. 0:54 – 1:09 Look at your team Now look at your team. Where would it help to strengthen planning, clear handoffs or checking an agent's result? Those are useful capabilities to develop, based on this example and the evidence in the Speaker notes. 1:09 – 1:26 Take one process And before Monday, do the smallest version of all of this. Pick one recurring process in your team, mark which steps an agent could run, and decide for each whether a person stays in, on or out of the loop.

One whole workflow 0:00 – 0:20 One whole workflow Let's bring the Episode together with the actual summer-party Workflow. Its goal is to bring 200 people from five offices together next summer, within €60,000. It moves through Plan, Requirements, Research and Page to a one-page party plan. The oversight choices shown are examples, not defaults. 0:20 – 0:40 In, on or out per step The labels are illustrative choices for this Workflow: Plan and Research are on the loop; Requirements and Page are in the loop. People choose a suitable level for each task, considering its risks, checks and context. Out means no intervention during that task, not necessarily no later review. 0:40 – 1:00 A contract at every handoff The cards make three handoffs visible: what the next stage receives, what it should deliver and how the result can be checked. Here, the organiser signs off the research questions; sources support the findings, and gaps stay open. Checks can be automated or human where appropriate. 1:00 – 1:28 Designed around the goal Notice that this example starts from the party goal, not from the org chart. Use Conway's law as a prompt to examine whether team boundaries help or hinder the goal; it is not a diagnosis by itself. Breaking work down, writing clear handoffs and checking results are useful capabilities to consider, not a universal checklist. Start with one process and decide what fits its tasks.
